Four organs that make their sound in three different ways. The **Hammond B-3** (1954) spins 91 metal tonewheels past pickups,
so each pitch is close to a pure sine, and mixes nine of them per key with **drawbars**. The **Vox Continental** (1962) and the
**Farfisa Combo Compact** (1964) are transistor *combo organs*: twelve oscillators for the top octave, divided down for every
octave below, so every note is equal-tempered and the tone colours are fixed by circuits. A **pipe organ** blows wind through
ranks of pipes, one rank a stop. The pipe organ here is **not any real instrument**: it is a small, made-up two-manual stop list.

Every fact about the real instruments is cited at the foot of the page; anything else (voicings, levels, panel positions) is this
page's own and is listed under each panel as "Not checked against the real instrument". Nobody has compared these sounds with the
real organs.

## The organs

<div class="ocmp" data-from="b3" data-to="pipe"></div>

**How to use it.** Pick **From** and **To**, choose an **Example**, then **▶ Play** (the first organ) or **▶ Play the translation**.
Pull a drawbar or press a tab on the top panel: the bottom one follows, and the report says for each rank
<span class="ocmp-exact">the same</span>, <span class="ocmp-approx">close</span> or <span class="ocmp-lost">cannot be done</span>.
Play from the keys under the panel or the computer keys a w s e d f t g y h u j k; **Keys play** picks the manual. **Panel / Simple**
switches the drawing for plain sliders; **☾ Dark / ☀ Light** changes the panel's background on every page.

## How the four make sound

- **Footage.** Every organ names its pitches by the length of an open pipe: 8′ is the note you press, 16′ an octave below, 4′ an
  octave above, 2⅔′ a twelfth above (Wikipedia, "Organ stop"). A B-3 drawbar, a Vox drawbar, a Farfisa tab and a pipe-organ stop all
  speak in footages, so the translation goes footage by footage.
- **Tonewheels are not quite in tune with themselves.** On the B-3 the 2⅔′ and 1⅗′ come from other wheels in equal temperament, not
  pure harmonics: the 1⅗′ of A4 sounds 2218 Hz, not 2200 (Electric Druid, via the band's organ notes). On the divide-down organs and
  the pipe organ here every pitch is equal-tempered too, but of the key's own top-octave oscillator.
- **Levels or switches.** Drawbars have nine positions (0 silent, each step about 3 dB); tabs and stops are only on or off. A level
  that a tab cannot make becomes "close".
- **Manuals.** The B-3 and the pipe organ have two manuals and pedals; the Vox and Farfisa have one manual. A registration's lower
  manual and pedals have nowhere to go on a combo organ.
- **Effects belong to the instrument.** The B-3's scanner vibrato / chorus (V1-V3, C1-C3), percussion and the Leslie's rotating horn
  and drum; the Vox's single vibrato; the Farfisa's four vibrato settings and reverb; the pipe organ's tremulant and its building.

## The B-3's switches

- **Preset keys.** The reverse-coloured octave left of each manual: **C** cancels (silence), **C♯ to A** are presets wired inside the
  organ, **A♯** and **B** switch to the two sets of drawbars (Wikipedia, "Hammond organ").
- **Percussion** adds a decaying 2nd or 3rd harmonic to the start of a note, soft or normal, fast or slow; it works only on the upper
  manual with preset key **B**, and silences the 1′ drawbar while on (Hammond XK-5 manual, which says this is the same as on the B-3 / C-3).
  It is *single-trigger*: it sounds again only after every key is let go (Wikipedia).
- **Leslie 122.** Slow (chorale) or fast (tremolo); horn and drum change speed at different rates. The speeds are measured figures from
  a 147 (the band's organ notes); the speed-up times are one forum post.

## What is not modelled

Tonewheel leakage between wheels and tapering, the Leslie cabinet's reflections and its amplifier, the B-3's pedal tone and the
pedal-board range, the Continental's bass-octave switch on later models, Farfisa's other models (Mini Compact, Compact Duo, Deluxe),
the pipe organ's wind (a shaky supply, pipes pulling each other's pitch), and any particular building.
